message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Doing it yourself the first time is very manageable with a small room like this. Here's everything in order.

## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it**, so there's a small ledge where they meet. You can feel it with bare feet, and low light from a window shows it up as shadowed ridges.

It matters with your tiles because long rectangular tiles (30 × 60 cm) are often very slightly bowed, a bit higher in the middle than at the ends. If you stagger them in a brick pattern with each row shifted by half a tile, the high middle of one tile lands next to the low end of its neighbour, and you get lippage. Two ways to avoid it:

- **Shift each row by a third of a tile (about 20 cm), not half.**
- **Use a tile levelling clip system.** These are cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets, and they're very beginner-friendly.

## Grout colour

**Go a shade or two darker than the tile: a mid grey.** It blends with pale grey porcelain and hides everyday dirt. White or very light grout on a floor is what looks grubby after a month.

Look for a stain-resistant or "easy-clean" grout, or seal ordinary grout once it's cured. It makes a noticeable difference in a bathroom.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first, then the toilet.** The tiles run neatly underneath, so you avoid fiddly cuts around the curved base, and the toilet sits on the finished floor.

Before you start, check the pan connector (the pipe joining the toilet to the waste outlet) will still fit, since the floor will be slightly higher. A longer or adjustable connector solves it if not.

## How many boxes

**Buy 4 boxes.**

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 m × 1.8 m | 4.32 m² |
| One tile | 0.3 m × 0.6 m | 0.18 m² |
| Tiles needed | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 | 24 tiles |
| Plus 10% | 24 × 1.1 | 26.4, so 27 tiles |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 | 3.4, so 4 boxes (32 tiles) |

Three boxes would be exactly 24 tiles with nothing spare, which isn't enough. Four leaves a few spares. That's useful because you'll lose more than you expect to practice cuts on a first job, and it's worth keeping two or three for future repairs.

**Check the batch or shade number on every box** before you leave the shop. Tiles from different batches can be slightly different colours.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for the bathroom floor this Saturday morning, roughly [9am–12pm], so there'll be some noise from the tile cutter. We'll keep it to the morning as best we can.
>
> Thank you as well for being so patient with the skip on the drive these past couple of weeks. It should be gone soon. If the noise is a problem for any reason, just knock and let us know.
>
> [Your names, house number]

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Get the floor flat and solid before anything else.** Check it with a long spirit level or straight edge, and fill dips first. If it's a timber floor, screw down tile backer board or exterior-grade ply over it. Floorboards flex, and flexing is what cracks tiles and grout.

2. **Lay the tiles out dry before you mix any adhesive.** Plan the layout so you don't end up with thin slivers at the doorway or along the most visible wall. Then start at the wall furthest from the door and work back towards it, so you don't tile yourself in.

3. **Use enough adhesive, and check it.** For tiles this size, spread adhesive on the floor with a notched trowel and butter a thin layer on the back of each tile too. Every so often, lift a freshly laid tile to check the back is almost fully covered. Hollow spots crack later. Mix small batches, and leave the adhesive to set for at least 24 hours before grouting.

The videos make it look smooth because the people in them have done it hundreds of times. Going slowly and checking as you go matters far more than speed.
